claims.text: A tungsten-rich refractory HEA engineered to reduce elements that form long-lived radioactive isotopes will exhibit low activation.
The proposed tungsten-rich refractory HEA will retain high-temperature structural integrity in fusion plasma-facing components.
The initial alloy is fully dense.
The initial alloy has a uniform microstructure.
Minimizing elements susceptible to high activation will reduce the alloy's irradiation-induced activation.
A stabilized, phase-homogeneous microstructure and its grain boundaries govern the alloy's mechanical strength.
A stabilized, phase-homogeneous microstructure and its grain boundaries govern radiation-induced activation behavior.
Tungsten and selected refractory metals contribute to high-temperature strength.
Tungsten and selected refractory metals limit the formation of long-lived radioactive isotopes.
Limiting the formation of long-lived radioactive isotopes reduces activation.
The selected refractory-metal composition maintains structural integrity under irradiation.
The proposed HEA will have superior high-temperature mechanical performance compared with conventional tungsten-based materials.
The proposed HEA will exhibit less induced radioactivity than conventional tungsten-based materials.
Pure tungsten may experience higher activation levels than the proposed HEA.

contradictions.description: Describing the material as both homogenized and in the as-cast state is internally ambiguous: homogenization ordinarily implies post-casting thermal processing, whereas 'as-cast' ordinarily excludes such processing.

The structural mediator attributes activation behavior to grain boundaries and phase homogeneity, while the mechanism attributes reduced activation to elemental selection and suppression of long-lived isotope formation; no link reconciling these distinct causal accounts is provided.
